problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.desc:
Given an integer list `nums`, return `True` if some value occurs **two or more times**, and `False` if every value is unique.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^5`
- `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
problems.starter:
def contains_duplicate(nums: List[int]) -> bool:
    pass
hints: A set lets you check whether you've seen a value before in O(1).
problems.explanation:
Walk the list once while keeping a set of values already seen. The first time a value is already in the set, a duplicate exists.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(n)

(Sorting and comparing neighbours also works in O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.)

quiz.q: What's the simplest O(n) check for duplicates?
options: Sort, then compare each element with the next one
quiz.why: A set drops duplicates, so its size shrinks exactly when a duplicate exists. Sorting works but is O(n log n); comparing sums fails on inputs like [0, 0].

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Contains Duplicate** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Contains Duplicate**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Contains Duplicate**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

grammar.title: Simple version: compare every pair
items: **Loop over indices:** `for i in range(len(nums)):` gives you `i = 0, 1, 2, …` up to the last index.
**Start a loop partway through:** `range(start, stop)`. For example, `range(i + 1, len(nums))` starts one past `i`.
**Nested loop:** put a second `for` indented inside the first.
**Access by index:** `nums[i]`, `nums[j]`
**Compare:** `if nums[i] == nums[j]:` (two equals signs compare; one equals sign assigns)
**Exit early:** `return True` inside the `if` ends the whole function right away.
**Fallback:** `return False` goes after both loops, at the function's indentation level, not inside a loop.
**Indentation is the structure:** each block (`for`, `if`) is indented 4 spaces deeper than the line that opens it.

grammar.title: Faster version: remember what you've seen
items: **Empty set:** `seen = set()` (not `{}`, which makes an empty dict).
**Membership:** `x in seen` gives `True` or `False`, in O(1).
**Add:** `seen.add(x)` puts a value in the set.
**Loop over values directly:** `for x in nums:` gives each value, with no indices.
**One-liner:** `len(set(nums)) != len(nums)`. A set drops duplicates, so it's shorter exactly when there was one.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.desc:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `True` if `t` is a rearrangement of the letters of `s` (each letter used exactly as many times), otherwise `False`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s), len(t) <= 5 * 10^4`
- Both strings contain lowercase English letters.
problems.starter:
def is_anagram(s: str, t: str) -> bool:
    pass
hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character appears the same number of times in both.
problems.explanation:
Count characters: add one for each char in `s`, subtract one for each char in `t`. If every count ends at zero, the strings are anagrams. (`Counter(s) == Counter(t)` is the one-liner.)

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(1) — at most 26 keys.

quiz.q: Two strings are anagrams exactly when…
options: Every character appears the same number of times in both
They have the same length and the same set of characters
Each character of one appears somewhere in the other
They have the same length and the same first letter
quiz.why: Their character counts must be equal, which you can check with `Counter(s) == Counter(t)`. Sets ignore counts: 'aab' and 'abb' have the same set.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Valid Anagram** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Valid Anagram**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Valid Anagram**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) — at most 26 keys.

grammar.title: Quick checks
items: **Length:** `len(s)` is the number of characters.
**Not equal:** `!=`. For example, `if len(s) != len(t): return False`.

grammar.title: Counting characters with a dict
items: **Empty dict:** `counts = {}`
**Loop over characters:** `for c in s:` gives one character at a time.
**Read with a default:** `counts.get(c, 0)` gives the stored count, or `0` if `c` isn't a key yet.
**Add one:** `counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1`
**Subtract one (for the other string):** `counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) - 1`
**Walk two strings side by side:** `for a, b in zip(s, t):` gives `a` from `s` and `b` from `t` at the same position.
**All the counts:** `counts.values()`
**Check every item:** `all(v == 0 for v in counts.values())` is `True` only if every count is zero.

grammar.title: Shortcuts
items: **Counter:** `Counter(s)` builds the count dict in one call (already imported). `Counter(s) == Counter(t)` compares two of them.
**Sorting:** `sorted(s)` returns the characters as a sorted list, so `sorted(s) == sorted(t)` also works (O(n log n)).

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.desc:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices** of the two different elements that add up to `target`.

Each input has exactly one valid answer. The two indices may be returned in either order.

**Constraints**
- `2 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^9 <= nums[i], target <= 10^9`
problems.starter:
def two_sum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: For each number x, the partner you need is target - x.
Store each value's index in a dict as you go so you can look up the partner in O(1).
problems.explanation:
Make one pass over the list with a hash map from each value to its index. For each element, check whether its complement `target - n` has already been seen; if so, we have the pair. Inserting *after* the check prevents using the same element twice.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(n)

quiz.q: Why insert `nums[i]` into the dict **after** checking for its complement?
options: So an element can't pair with itself
So a repeated value doesn't overwrite its earlier index
So each lookup stays O(1) as the dict grows
It doesn't matter; either order gives the same answer
quiz.why: With target 6 and x = 3, checking first stops 3 from matching itself.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Two Sum** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Two Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Two Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

grammar.title: Simple version: try every pair
items: **Outer loop:** `for i in range(len(nums)):`
**Inner loop starting after i:** `for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):`. Starting at `i + 1` means an element never pairs with itself.
**Check a pair:** `if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:`
**Return a list:** `return [i, j]` (square brackets build a list).

grammar.title: Faster version: a dict from value to index
items: **Empty dict:** `index_of = {}`
**Index and value together:** `for i, n in enumerate(nums):`
**The partner you need:** `need = target - n`
**Is it a key?** `need in index_of` gives `True`/`False` in O(1).
**Look it up:** `index_of[need]` gives the stored index.
**Store:** `index_of[n] = i`
**Order matters:** check for the partner first, then store `n`, so a number can't pair with itself.
**Fallback:** `return []` after the loop, so the function always returns something.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.desc:
Given a list of strings `strs`, group together the strings that are anagrams of one another. Return the groups in any order; strings within a group may also be in any order.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(strs) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= len(strs[i]) <= 100`, lowercase English letters
problems.starter:
def group_anagrams(strs: List[str]) -> List[List[str]]:
    pass
hints: Anagrams share the same sorted string (or the same 26-letter count tuple). Use that as a dict key.
problems.explanation:
Every anagram group shares a canonical key. Using a tuple of 26 letter counts as the key avoids sorting each word.

- **Time:** O(n · k) where k is the max word length (O(n · k log k) if you sort each word for the key)
- **Space:** O(n · k)

quiz.q: What makes a good dictionary key for grouping anagrams?
options: The sorted word, or a tuple of its 26 letter counts
The word's letters as a frozenset, ignoring order
The sum of the word's character codes, as an int
The word's length paired with its first letter
quiz.why: All anagrams map to the same canonical form. A frozenset loses counts ('aab' vs 'abb'), and code sums collide for different letters.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Group Anagrams** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Group Anagrams**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n · k) where k is the max word length (O(n · k log k) if you sort each word for the key).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Group Anagrams**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n · k).

grammar.title: Making a key that every anagram shares
items: **Sort a string:** `sorted("tea")` gives the list `['a', 'e', 't']`.
**Glue a list of strings:** `"".join(['a', 'e', 't'])` gives `"aet"`. Together: `"".join(sorted(s))`.
**Dict keys must be unchangeable:** strings and tuples can be keys, lists can't. `tuple(some_list)` converts.
**26 counters:** `count = [0] * 26` makes a list of 26 zeros.
**Letter to index:** `ord(c) - ord('a')` turns `'a'…'z'` into `0…25`, so `count[ord(c) - ord('a')] += 1` counts a letter.

grammar.title: Grouping
items: **Dict of lists:** `groups = defaultdict(list)` (already imported). A missing key starts as an empty list.
**Add to a group:** `groups[key].append(s)`, with no need to check whether the key exists.
**Plain-dict alternative:** `groups.setdefault(key, []).append(s)`
**The answer:** `list(groups.values())` turns all the groups into a list.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.desc:
Given an integer list `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` values that occur most often. The answer is guaranteed to be unique; return it in any order.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(nums) <= 10^5`
- `1 <= k <=` number of distinct values

**Follow-up:** can you beat O(n log n)?
problems.starter:
def top_k_frequent(nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: First count frequencies with a dict.
A frequency can be at most n, so you can bucket values by frequency and read buckets from high to low.
problems.explanation:
Count each value, then place values into buckets indexed by frequency (frequencies range 1..n). Scanning buckets from the highest frequency down collects the top `k` without sorting.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(n)

A heap of size k (`heapq.nlargest(k, count, key=count.get)`) is O(n log k) and also a fine answer.

quiz.q: How does bucket sort get top-k in O(n)?
options: Frequencies are at most n, so index buckets by frequency
Values are bounded, so index buckets by the value itself
It keeps a heap of size k while it counts
It only looks at the first k distinct values
quiz.why: Bucket i holds the values occurring i times; read the buckets from high to low. A size-k heap works too, but it's O(n log k).

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Top K Frequent Elements** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Top K Frequent Elements**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Top K Frequent Elements**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

grammar.title: Counting
items: **Count everything:** `count = Counter(nums)` maps each value to how often it appears.
**Loop over pairs:** `for value, freq in count.items():`

grammar.title: Simple version: sort by frequency
items: **Sort keys by their counts, biggest first:** `sorted(count, key=count.get, reverse=True)`
**Take the first k:** the slice `[:k]`.
**Built-in:** `count.most_common(k)` gives the k most common `(value, freq)` pairs. `[v for v, _ in count.most_common(k)]` keeps just the values.

grammar.title: Faster version: buckets indexed by frequency
items: **A list of separate empty lists:** `buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]`. (Don't write `[[]] * n`, which repeats the *same* list n times.)
**`_` for unused loop variables:** a convention for a variable you never read.
**Drop into a bucket:** `buckets[freq].append(value)`
**Count down:** `range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1)` goes from the last index down to 1. The third argument is the step.
**Collect and stop:** `result.append(value)`, then `if len(result) == k: return result`.

problems.title: Encode and Decode Strings
problems.desc:
Write `encode`, which turns a list of strings into a **single string**, and `decode`, which turns that string back into the original list.

The tests check that `decode(encode(strs)) == strs`. The strings can contain **any** characters, including `#`, digits, spaces, and empty strings, so a simple delimiter won't work on its own.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(strs) <= 200`
- `0 <= len(strs[i]) <= 200`
hints: Prefix each string with its length and a separator, e.g. `5#hello`. When decoding, read the length first, then exactly that many characters.
problems.explanation:
Use length-prefix encoding: write `len(s)`, a `#`, then `s` itself. When decoding, read digits up to the first `#`, which gives the length, then slice exactly that many characters. Since we never search *inside* a string's contents, any characters are safe.

- **Time:** O(total characters)
- **Space:** O(total characters)

quiz.q: Why does `len + '#' + s` encoding survive strings that contain `#`?
options: The decoder reads the length, then slices exactly that many characters
The decoder splits on '#' and rejoins pieces that look too short
The encoder escapes each '#' in the string as '##'
It doesn't; a '#' inside a string breaks it
quiz.why: Only the first '#' after the digits is a delimiter; the content is sliced by length, so its characters are never searched.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Encode and Decode Strings** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

grammar.title: Two functions
items: **Write both:** `def encode(strs):` and `def decode(s):` are separate functions, each with its own `return`.

grammar.title: Encoding
items: **f-strings:** `f"{len(s)}#{s}"` puts values inside a string. For `"abc"` it gives `"3#abc"`.
**Glue strings together:** `"".join(parts)` joins a list of strings with nothing between them.
**Join a generator:** `"".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)` builds each piece and joins them in one line.

grammar.title: Decoding
items: **Two variables at once:** `result, i = [], 0`
**A loop where you control the jumps:** `while i < len(s):`
**Find a character:** `s.index("#", i)` gives the index of the first `#` at or after position `i`.
**Slice:** `s[i:j]` is the text from `i` up to, but not including, `j`.
**Text to number:** `int("12")` gives `12`, so `length = int(s[i:j])`.
**Take exactly length characters:** `s[j + 1 : j + 1 + length]`
**Jump past them:** `i = j + 1 + length`

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.desc:
Given an integer list `nums`, return a list `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` **except** `nums[i]`.

Solve it in O(n) time **without using division**.

**Constraints**
- `2 <= len(nums) <= 10^5`
- `-30 <= nums[i] <= 30`
problems.starter:
def product_except_self(nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: answer[i] is the product of everything to the left of i multiplied by the product of everything to the right of i.
Compute prefix products in one pass and suffix products in a second pass.
problems.solution:
def product_except_self(nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        answer[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        answer[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return answer
problems.explanation:
Fill `answer[i]` with the product of everything left of `i` (running prefix), then sweep from the right multiplying in the running suffix product.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(1) extra (the output doesn't count)

quiz.q: answer[i] equals…
options: prefix product before i × suffix product after i
prefix product up to and including i × suffix product after i
quiz.why: That avoids division, so it also works when the array contains zeros.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Product of Array Except Self** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Product of Array Except Self**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Product of Array Except Self**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) extra (the output doesn't count).

grammar.title: Setting up
items: **Length:** `n = len(nums)`
**A list of ones:** `answer = [1] * n`

grammar.title: Left-to-right pass
items: **Loop forwards:** `for i in range(n):`
**Store the running product so far:** `answer[i] = prefix` (start with `prefix = 1`).
**Multiply in place:** `prefix *= nums[i]` is short for `prefix = prefix * nums[i]`.

grammar.title: Right-to-left pass
items: **Loop backwards:** `range(n - 1, -1, -1)` gives `n-1, n-2, …, 0`. The stop is `-1` because the stop is never included.
**Same thing, more readable:** `for i in reversed(range(n)):`
**Multiply into the answer:** `answer[i] *= suffix`, then `suffix *= nums[i]`.

grammar.title: Note
items: **No division needed:** `/` always gives a float in Python and fails on zeros; this approach avoids it.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.desc:
Given an unsorted integer list `nums`, return the length of the longest run of **consecutive integers** (like 4, 5, 6, 7) whose values all appear in `nums`. The values can appear anywhere in the list.

Aim for O(n) time.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^5`
- `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
problems.starter:
def longest_consecutive(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    pass
hints: Put everything in a set.
Only start counting from x if x - 1 is NOT in the set. That way each run is counted once.
problems.explanation:
With all values in a set, a number starts a sequence only if `x - 1` is absent. From each start, extend upward while `x + length` exists. Each number is visited at most twice overall, so the work stays linear.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(n)

quiz.q: Why only start counting from x when `x - 1` isn't in the set?
options: So each run is walked once, keeping the total O(n)
So runs of negative numbers are counted correctly
So counting starts at the smallest value in the array
So duplicate values in nums are ignored
quiz.why: x − 1 missing means x starts a run. Starting mid-run would re-walk the same sequence many times.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Longest Consecutive Sequence** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Arrays & Hashing** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Longest Consecutive Sequence**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Longest Consecutive Sequence**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

grammar.title: Simple version: sort first
items: **Sort:** `nums.sort()` sorts in place; `sorted(nums)` returns a new list.
**Compare with the previous item:** `nums[i] == nums[i - 1] + 1` continues a run; `nums[i] == nums[i - 1]` is a duplicate to skip.
**Empty input:** `if not nums: return 0` (an empty list counts as false).

grammar.title: Faster version: a set
items: **Set from a list:** `values = set(nums)` drops duplicates and gives O(1) lookups.
**Not in:** `x - 1 not in values` is the opposite of `in`.
**Loop over the set:** `for x in values:`
**Count up a run:** `while x + length in values: length += 1` repeats as long as the condition holds.
**Keep the best:** `best = max(best, length)`, starting from `best = 0`.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.desc:
A phrase is a palindrome if, after lowercasing it and removing every character that isn't a letter or digit, it reads the same forwards and backwards.

Given a string `s`, return `True` if it is a palindrome, otherwise `False`.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(s) <= 2 * 10^5`
- `s` contains printable ASCII characters.
problems.starter:
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    pass
hints: Use one pointer at each end. Skip characters that aren't alphanumeric (`str.isalnum`).
problems.explanation:
Two pointers move inward from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercase forms. This avoids building a cleaned copy.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(1)

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

quiz.q: How do you avoid building a cleaned copy of the string?
options: Move two pointers inward, skipping non-alphanumeric characters
Compare s with s[::-1], ignoring non-alphanumeric characters
Lowercase s in place first, then compare its two ends
Use a regex to test whether it reads the same both ways
quiz.why: Two pointers give O(1) extra space. `s[::-1]` builds a copy, and strings can't be changed in place.

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **Valid Palindrome** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Two Pointers** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Valid Palindrome**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Valid Palindrome**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

grammar.title: Simple version: clean, then compare
items: **Filter and lowercase:** `cleaned = "".join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())`
**Reverse a string:** `cleaned[::-1]` is a reversed copy, so `return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]`.

grammar.title: Two pointers (no copy)
items: **Both ends:** `left, right = 0, len(s) - 1` (the last index is `len - 1`).
**Until they meet:** `while left < right:`
**Move inward:** `left += 1`, `right -= 1`
**Letter or digit?** `c.isalnum()`. `not` flips it: `not s[left].isalnum()` is `True` for spaces and punctuation.
**Skip junk:** `while left < right and not s[left].isalnum(): left += 1`. `and` stops early, so keep the bound check first.
**Case-insensitive compare:** `s[left].lower() != s[right].lower()`
**Exit and fallback:** `return False` on a mismatch; `return True` after the loop.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.desc:
Given an integer list `nums`, return every **unique** triplet `[a, b, c]` of values taken from three different positions such that `a + b + c == 0`.

The output must not contain duplicate triplets. Triplets, and the numbers inside them, may be in any order.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 3000`
- `-10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`
problems.starter:
def three_sum(nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
    pass
hints: Sort first.
Fix the first number, then run a two-pointer search for the other two on the rest of the list.
Skip equal neighbouring values to avoid duplicate triplets.
problems.explanation:
After sorting, fix `a = nums[i]` and look for a pair summing to `-a` in the remaining suffix with two pointers. Skip repeated values of `a` and repeated `lo` values after a match to keep triplets unique.

- **Time:** O(n²)
- **Space:** O(1) extra besides the sort/output

quiz.q: In the O(n²) solution, after sorting and fixing `nums[i]`, how are the other two found?
options: Two pointers moving inward over the rest
Binary search for each partner in the rest of the array
A nested loop over every remaining pair
A min-heap of the remaining values
quiz.why: Two pointers find all pairs in O(n) per i, so O(n²) overall. Binary search per partner is O(n² log n); a nested loop is O(n³).

quiz.q: Which technique does the standard solution to **3Sum** use?
quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Two Pointers** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **3Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n²).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **3Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) extra besides the sort/output.

grammar.title: Sorting
items: **Sorted copy:** `nums = sorted(nums)` (or `nums.sort()` to sort in place).

grammar.title: Outer loop
items: **Index and value:** `for i, a in enumerate(nums):`
**Stop the loop entirely:** `break`. For example, `if a > 0: break`, since everything after is positive too.
**Skip to the next round:** `continue`. For example, `if i > 0 and a == nums[i - 1]: continue` skips a repeated first value.

items: **Set them:** `lo, hi = i + 1, len(nums) - 1`
**Loop:** `while lo < hi:`
**Three-way branch:** `if total < 0: … elif total > 0: … else: …` (`elif` means "else if").
**List of lists:** `result.append([a, nums[lo], nums[hi]])`

quiz.q: With a dict of last-seen indexes, when a repeated char is found inside the window, where does `left` jump?
options: Just past that char's previous index
To the current index, starting a new window
One position right of where it is now

grammar.title: Window basics
items: **Set two variables to 0:** `left = best = 0` (fine for numbers; don't do this with lists).
**Right edge and character:** `for right, c in enumerate(s):`
**Window length:** `right - left + 1`
**Keep the best:** `best = max(best, right - left + 1)`

grammar.title: Option A: a set of what's in the window
items: **Empty set:** `window = set()`
**Shrink until c is gone:** `while c in window: window.remove(s[left]); left += 1`
**Add the new character:** `window.add(c)`

grammar.title: Option B: a dict of last-seen positions
items: **Empty dict:** `last_seen = {}`
**Jump left past a repeat:** `if c in last_seen and last_seen[c] >= left: left = last_seen[c] + 1`
**Record the position:** `last_seen[c] = right`

options: window length − count of its most common char ≤ k
window length − count of its least common char ≤ k
the number of distinct chars in it is ≤ k + 1

items: **Several zeros at once:** `left = top = best = 0`
**Right edge and character:** `for right, c in enumerate(s):`
**Count in a dict:** `count = {}`, then `count[c] = count.get(c, 0) + 1`.
**Most common so far:** `top = max(top, count[c])`. Or `max(count.values())` gives it directly (at most 26 keys, so it's cheap).
**Window length:** `right - left + 1`
**Replacements needed:** `(right - left + 1) - top`

grammar.title: Shrinking
items: **Shrink while too many:** `while (right - left + 1) - top > k:`
**Drop the left character:** `count[s[left]] -= 1`, then `left += 1`.

problems.desc:

The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(s), len(t) <= 10^5`
- Upper- and lowercase English letters.

def min_window(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    pass
hints: Count what t needs. Expand right until the window satisfies every count.
Then shrink from the left as much as possible while it still satisfies every count, recording the best window.
problems.explanation:
`need` tracks how many of each character the window still lacks (negative means surplus), and `missing` counts how many required characters are still missing. Expand `right`; once `missing == 0` the window is valid, so shrink from the left while recording the smallest window, and stop when removing a char makes it invalid again.

- **Time:** O(|s| + |t|)
- **Space:** O(alphabet)

quiz.q: When do you shrink the window from the left?
options: While it still contains all the required characters
Whenever it grows longer than t, to keep it short
Whenever a character in the window repeats
Only once `right` has reached the end of s
quiz.why: Keep shrinking while it is still valid, recording the best window as you go.

quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Sliding Window** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

grammar.title: What you still need
items: **Count the target:** `need = Counter(t)`. A Counter returns 0 for a missing key, so `need[c]` never raises a KeyError (a plain dict would).
**Characters still missing:** `missing = len(t)`

grammar.title: Growing the window
items: **Right edge:** `for right, c in enumerate(s):`
**Did this character help?** `if need[c] > 0: missing -= 1`
**Use it up:** `need[c] -= 1` (it can go negative, which just means extras).

grammar.title: Shrinking while valid
items: **Loop while the window has everything:** `while missing == 0:`
**Record the best as a tuple:** `best = (right - left + 1, left, right + 1)`. Read parts with `best[0]`, `best[1]`, `best[2]`.
**Start best as "nothing yet":** `best = (float("inf"), 0, 0)`
**Give back the left character:** `need[s[left]] += 1`, then `if need[s[left]] > 0: missing += 1`, then `left += 1`.

grammar.title: Returning
items: **One-line if/else:** `"" if best[0] == float("inf") else s[best[1]:best[2]]`

# Definition for singly-linked list (pre-defined):
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

def reverse_list(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    pass
hints: Walk the list keeping a `prev` pointer. For each node, point `node.next` back at `prev`.
problems.solution:
def reverse_list(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev
problems.explanation:
Iteratively flip each `next` pointer. Save `cur.next` before overwriting it, then advance. When `cur` falls off the end, `prev` is the new head.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(1) (recursive version uses O(n) stack)

options: head, so you can return it at the end
quiz.why: Otherwise you lose your only reference to the remaining nodes. At the end, prev is the new head.

items: **Fields:** `node.val` is the value, `node.next` is the next node, and `None` marks the end.
**Walk until the end:** `while cur:` stops once `cur` is `None`.

grammar.title: Iterative reversal
items: **Start:** `prev = None`, `cur = head`
**Save the rest first:** `nxt = cur.next`
**Point backwards:** `cur.next = prev`
**Step forward:** `prev = cur`, then `cur = nxt`.
**New head:** `return prev`
**All at once:** `cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next`. The whole right side is evaluated before anything is assigned.

grammar.title: Recursive version
items: **Base case:** `if not head or not head.next: return head`
**Recurse:** `new_head = reverse_list(head.next)`
**Flip one link:** `head.next.next = head`, then `head.next = None`, then `return new_head`.

problems.desc:
Given a linked list `L0 → L1 → … → Ln-1 → Ln`, rearrange it **in place** to

`L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → …`

Change the links between nodes, not the values. Return nothing; the tests inspect the list starting from the original head.

**Constraints**
- `1 <=` number of nodes `<= 5 * 10^4`


_Linked lists are shown as Python lists in the examples; your function receives and returns `ListNode` objects._
problems.starter:
# Definition for singly-linked list (pre-defined):
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

def reorder_list(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    pass
hints: Find the middle of the list with slow and fast pointers.
Reverse the second half.
Merge the two halves by alternating nodes.
problems.solution:
def reorder_list(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    second = slow.next
    slow.next = None
    prev = None
    while second:
        second.next, prev, second = prev, second, second.next
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        n1, n2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = n1
        first, second = n1, n2
problems.explanation:
The solution has three classic steps: (1) find the midpoint with slow/fast pointers and cut the list there; (2) reverse the second half; (3) interleave nodes from the first half and the reversed second half.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(1)

quiz.q: What are the three steps?

Find the middle, reverse the first half, interleave the halves
Reverse the whole list, then interleave it with the original
Find the middle, reverse the second half, append it to the first
quiz.why: Each step is O(n) time and O(1) space. Reversing the whole list in place destroys the original order you need.

problems.desc:
You are given a list of `k` linked lists, each sorted ascending. Merge them all into one sorted linked list and return its head.

**Constraints**

- Each list has `0..500` nodes.


_Linked lists are shown as Python lists in the examples; your function receives and returns `ListNode` objects._
problems.starter:
# Definition for singly-linked list (pre-defined):
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

def merge_k_lists(lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    pass
hints: Put the head of every list into a min-heap.
Pop the smallest, append it, and push its `next`. Use (value, index, node) tuples so ties don't compare nodes.
problems.solution:
def merge_k_lists(lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
    heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        _, i, node = heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next
problems.explanation:
A min-heap always holds the current smallest unmerged node from each list. Each of the N total nodes is pushed and popped once.

- **Time:** O(N log k)
- **Space:** O(k)

Pairwise divide-and-conquer merging (merge lists 0+1, 2+3, …) has the same complexity.

quiz.q: Why push `(val, i, node)` into the heap instead of `(val, node)`?
options: Ties on val would compare ListNodes, which raises TypeError
So nodes from the same list keep their original order
Because heapq orders tuples by their last item first
Because ListNodes can't be hashed without an index
quiz.why: The unique index i breaks ties before Python ever compares nodes.

items: **Push:** `heappush(heap, item)`. **Pop the smallest:** `heappop(heap)`. **Peek:** `heap[0]`.

**Tuples compare item by item:** push `(node.val, i, node)`. The index `i` breaks ties, so two `ListNode`s are never compared (that raises a TypeError).
**Build with a filter:** `[(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]` skips empty lists.
**Unpack and ignore:** `_, i, node = heappop(heap)`
**Refill from the same list:** `if node.next: heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))`
**Dummy head:** `dummy = tail = ListNode()`, then `return dummy.next`.

problems.desc:
There are `num_courses` courses labelled `0` to `num_courses - 1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prerequisites` means you must take course `b` before course `a`.

Return `True` if it's possible to finish every course.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= num_courses <= 2000`
- `0 <= len(prerequisites) <= 5000`; all pairs are distinct.
problems.starter:
def can_finish(num_courses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
    pass
hints: This is cycle detection in a directed graph.
Use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with zero remaining prerequisites. If you can take all of them, there's no cycle.
problems.explanation:
Use a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm). Start with courses that have no prerequisites; taking one lowers the in-degree of the courses that depend on it. If a cycle exists, some courses never reach in-degree 0.

- **Time:** O(V + E)
- **Space:** O(V + E)

DFS with three colours (unvisited / visiting / done) is the other standard approach.

quiz.q: What does it mean if the topological sort processes fewer courses than exist?
options: There's a cycle, so it's impossible
The graph is disconnected, so it needs another pass
Some prerequisites were listed more than once
The courses can still all be finished in another order
quiz.why: Courses on a cycle never reach in-degree 0. Disconnected parts are fine; Kahn's starts from every in-degree-0 node.

quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Graphs** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Course Schedule**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(V + E).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Course Schedule**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(V + E).

grammar.title: Building the graph
items: **Adjacency list:** `graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]`
**Counts:** `indegree = [0] * num_courses`
**Unpack each pair:** `for course, pre in prerequisites:`
**Add an edge:** `graph[pre].append(course)`, then `indegree[course] += 1`.

grammar.title: Topological order (Kahn's algorithm)
items: **Queue of courses with no prerequisites:** `queue = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)`
**Take one:** `cur = queue.popleft()`, then `taken += 1`.
**Unlock what it leads to:** `for nxt in graph[cur]: indegree[nxt] -= 1`, and `if indegree[nxt] == 0: queue.append(nxt)`.
**Return a comparison directly:** `return taken == num_courses`

grammar.title: DFS alternative
items: **States per course:** `state = [0] * num_courses` (0 = new, 1 = in progress, 2 = done). Seeing a 1 again means a cycle.

problems.title: Graph Valid Tree
problems.desc:
You have `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of undirected `edges`. Return `True` if these edges form a valid **tree**: the graph is connected and contains no cycles.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= n <= 2000`
- No duplicate edges or self-loops.
problems.starter:
def valid_tree(n: int, edges: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
    pass
hints: A tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges.
With exactly n - 1 edges, the graph is a tree if and only if it is connected (equivalently, if it has no cycle). Union-find or DFS can check this.

Reject immediately unless there are exactly `n - 1` edges. Then run union-find: if any edge joins two nodes that are already connected, it forms a cycle. With `n - 1` edges and no cycle, the graph must be connected.

- **Time:** O(n · α(n))
- **Space:** O(n)

quiz.q: A graph with n nodes and n − 1 edges is a tree if and only if…
options: It's connected (equivalently, it has no cycle)
Every node has at least one edge, so none is isolated
Every node has at most two edges
No node has more than n − 2 edges
quiz.why: With n − 1 edges, connected and acyclic imply each other. A triangle plus a separate 3-node path has n − 1 edges and no isolated node, but isn't connected.

quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Graphs** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Graph Valid Tree**?

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Graph Valid Tree**?

grammar.title: Quick check
items: **A tree has exactly n − 1 edges:** `if len(edges) != n - 1: return False`

grammar.title: Union-find
items: **Everyone is their own parent:** `parent = list(range(n))` gives `[0, 1, …, n-1]`.
**Find the root:** `def find(x):` with `while parent[x] != x: x = parent[x]`, then `return x`.
**Path compression (optional speed-up):** `parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]` inside that loop.
**Changing a list from a helper:** `parent[...] = …` works without `nonlocal`.
**Unpack each edge:** `for a, b in edges:`
**Two finds at once:** `ra, rb = find(a), find(b)`
**Same root means a cycle:** `if ra == rb: return False`
**Union:** `parent[ra] = rb`

grammar.title: DFS alternative
items: **Undirected adjacency:** `graph = defaultdict(list)`, with both `graph[a].append(b)` and `graph[b].append(a)`.
**Everything reached?** `len(seen) == n`

items: **Start:** `parent = list(range(n))`, `components = n`
**Find:** `def find(x):` with `while parent[x] != x: x = parent[x]`, then `return x`.
**Each edge:** `for a, b in edges:`, then `ra, rb = find(a), find(b)`.
**Merge two groups:** `if ra != rb: parent[ra] = rb; components -= 1`

grammar.title: DFS alternative
items: **Undirected adjacency:** `graph = defaultdict(list)`, adding each edge both ways.
**Visited set:** `seen = set()`
**Count starts:** `for node in range(n): if node not in seen:`, add 1 and explore everything reachable.

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.desc:
An alien language uses lowercase English letters in an unknown order. You're given `words`, a list of words from its dictionary **already sorted** by the alien ordering.

Return a string containing every distinct letter that appears in `words`, arranged in an order consistent with the dictionary. If several orders work, return any of them. If no valid order exists, return `""`.

Ordering is lexicographic: the first position where two words differ decides which comes first. If one word is a prefix of the other, the shorter word comes first.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(words) <= 100`, `1 <= len(words[i]) <= 100`
problems.starter:
def alien_order(words: List[str]) -> str:
    pass
hints: Compare each pair of adjacent words. The first differing letters give one edge: a comes before b.
Watch for the invalid case where a longer word comes before its own prefix (e.g. 'abc' before 'ab').
Topologically sort the letters; a cycle means there's no valid order.
problems.explanation:
Build a graph over letters: for each adjacent pair of words, the first mismatch gives the edge `x → y`. If the pairs never differ and the first word is longer, the input is invalid. Then use Kahn's topological sort; if not every letter gets output, there's a cycle.

- **Time:** O(C), where C is the total number of characters across all words
- **Space:** O(U + edges), where U is the number of unique letters (≤ 26)

quiz.q: What does one adjacent word pair tell you?
options: The first differing characters give one ordering edge
Every position where they differ gives an ordering edge
Their first characters give one ordering edge
Nothing, unless both words have the same length
quiz.why: Characters after the first difference carry no information, and equal first characters say nothing.

quiz.why: The standard solution uses the **Advanced Graphs** pattern. The pattern guide explains how to recognise it.

grammar.title: Every letter
items: **Dict comprehension over two loops:** `graph = {c: set() for w in words for c in w}` creates a key for every letter that appears.
**Loop over a dict's keys:** `indegree = {c: 0 for c in graph}`

grammar.title: Comparing neighbouring words
items: **Adjacent pairs:** `for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]):` gives `(words[0], words[1])`, `(words[1], words[2])`, …
**Letter by letter:** `for x, y in zip(a, b):`. It stops at the shorter word.
**First difference:** `if x != y:`, add the edge, then `break`.
**Don't double-count:** `if y not in graph[x]: graph[x].add(y); indegree[y] += 1`
**`for … else`:** the `else:` block runs only if the loop finished *without* `break`. Here that means one word is a prefix of the other, and `if len(a) > len(b): return ""`.

grammar.title: Topological order
items: **Start queue:** `deque(sorted(c for c in indegree if indegree[c] == 0))`. `sorted` gives a predictable order.
**Process:** `c = queue.popleft()`, `order.append(c)`, then lower each neighbour's indegree.
**Cycle check and answer:** `return "".join(order) if len(order) == len(graph) else ""`

problems.desc:

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(intervals) <= 10^4`

problems.starter:

hints: Work in three phases: copy the intervals that end before the new one starts, merge every interval that overlaps it, then copy the rest.
problems.solution:
def insert(intervals: List[List[int]], new_interval: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
    result = []
    start, end = new_interval
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < start:
        result.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= end:
        start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
        end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append([start, end])
    result.extend(intervals[i:])
    return result
problems.explanation:
Because the input is sorted, a single scan works. Intervals ending before `start` come first unchanged. Intervals that start at or before `end` overlap and get absorbed into the new interval. The rest follow unchanged.

- **Time:** O(n)
- **Space:** O(n) for the output

items: **Sum without carries:** `a ^ b`
**The carries:** `(a & b) << 1`
**Repeat until no carry:** `while b:` with `a, b = a ^ b, (a & b) << 1`. This alone works for non-negative numbers.

grammar.title: 32-bit masking for negatives
items: **Python ints never overflow,** so negative numbers would loop forever. Keep only 32 bits.
**Hex literal for 32 ones:** `mask = 0xFFFFFFFF`
**Trim:** `(a ^ b) & mask` and `((a & b) << 1) & mask`
**Largest positive 32-bit number:** `0x7FFFFFFF`. Anything above it is a negative number in 32-bit.
**Back to a Python negative:** `~(a ^ mask)`. `~x` equals `-x - 1`.
**One-line if/else:** `return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ mask)`
